title: Iran Sets Seven Demands for Hormuz; ADNOC Vessel Missiled in Strait; Senate Targets Russian Oil Buyers With 100% Tariff Threat
subhead: Iran laid out sweeping conditions to reopen the Strait of Hormuz — including lifting sanctions and withdrawing US forces — while an Iranian missile struck a UAE-linked tanker transiting the strait. Meanwhile, the US Senate passed a sweeping sanctions bill threatening 100% tariffs on countries buying Russian oil, and Trump announced a $3 billion push on critical minerals to counter China and replenish weapons stockpiles depleted by the Iran war.

sections.heading: Iran Demands US Concessions to Reopen Hormuz, Missiles ADNOC Tanker
sections.body:
Iran's Supreme National Security Council said on Saturday that the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until the United States 'corrects its behaviour,' issuing seven conditions for reopening the waterway. The demands, published by state broadcaster IRIB and attributed to council secretary and IRGC commander Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, include: permanently ending the war with Iran and its allied groups; never threatening Iran again; lifting the naval blockade of Iranian ports; withdrawing US military forces from the region; compensating Iran for war damage; lifting all sanctions; and unconditionally releasing frozen Iranian assets. There was no immediate US response.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran was close to a separate agreement with Oman on managing the strait, particularly on establishing a transit route for vessels. But he stressed that reopening the waterway depended on other conditions and accused the US of violating the June interim agreement. Oman called the talks 'positive and constructive' but condemned attacks on shipping.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard separately stated that reopening Hormuz 'does not depend' on the Oman negotiations, but on the US accepting Iran's conditions — underscoring internal tensions between diplomats and the IRGC over who controls the process. The 60-day window for final negotiations under the June interim deal expires in just over a week, though it could be extended.

Hours before Iran's statement, the UAE reported that an Iranian missile struck an ADNOC-owned vessel transiting the Strait of Hormuz. The UAE Foreign Ministry called it an act of piracy. ADNOC said more than a dozen of its vessels have been hit by missiles and drones since the war began, with one crew member killed and 20 injured in total. The UK Maritime Trade Operations Centre confirmed a vessel east of Oman's Khasab was hit by a projectile that caused a fire, later extinguished.

Iranian inflation has hit 88.6%, according to Iranian official Kazem Gharibabadi, who said negotiations were essential as the US blockade threatens to cripple the economy. Iran is betting that military pressure and energy market disruption will force a better deal, but the dual track of negotiating with Oman while attacking shipping is creating mixed signals.
sections.whyItMatters: Iran's maximalist conditions set the floor for any Hormuz deal far above what the US is likely to accept — particularly on troop withdrawal and sanctions relief. The ADNOC missile strike shows Iran is still willing to use force against Gulf states even as it negotiates, which risks pushing the UAE and Saudi Arabia further into the US camp. The IRGC's public dismissal of the Oman process suggests Iran's military leadership may overrule any diplomatic deal that doesn't meet all seven demands.

sections.heading: Senate Passes Graham Sanctions Bill, Threatens 100% Tariffs on Russian Oil Buyers
sections.body:
The US Senate voted 86-11 on Thursday to pass the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, renamed after Senator Lindsey Graham, who championed the bill before his death on July 11. The legislation authorises the president to impose up to 100% tariffs on goods from countries that are among the top five importers of Russian oil and gas — currently China, India, Azerbaijan, Hungary, and Slovakia.

The bill also extends the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996 — which penalises companies investing in Iran's energy sector — until 2031. It includes a presidential waiver clause allowing the president to certify that enforcement is not in the national interest.

The reaction from target countries was swift. Indian foreign affairs analyst Sushant Sareen of the Observer Research Foundation said India must now 'de-risk from the US' just as it has de-risked from China, calling the measure evidence that 'the US under Trump, and maybe even after Trump, will remain a hostile power.' He also questioned whether Washington would apply the same tariffs to China, noting: 'We have seen Trump impose tariffs on us, but not on China.'

India's crude oil import bill already surged 26% to $49 billion in Q1 FY2027 despite an 18% drop in volumes, driven by higher global prices from the Middle East conflict, according to NewsBytes. The bill now heads to the House of Representatives.
sections.whyItMatters: The Graham Act transforms secondary sanctions on Russian energy into a blunt tariff weapon that could hit India especially hard — a country Washington considers a strategic partner. The 100% tariff threat creates a direct clash between US alliance priorities and energy economics: India buys Russian oil because it's cheap, and replacing those volumes is difficult during a Gulf supply crisis. The presidential waiver clause gives Trump leverage to apply tariffs selectively, which could be used to extract trade concessions from India unrelated to Russia.

sections.heading: Trump Announces $3 Billion Critical Minerals Push to Counter China
sections.body:
President Trump announced a $3 billion government investment in critical minerals and battery projects at a State Department roundtable on Friday, attended by more than 200 mining executives, educators, and investors. The push is framed as both a national security imperative — replenishing weapons stockpiles depleted during the Iran war — and an industrial policy move to break dependence on Chinese supply chains.

Specific announcements included a $1.4 billion conditional loan from the Defense Department's Office of Strategic Capital for Sila Nanotechnologies, a lithium-ion battery components maker; a $400 million conditional loan to Sunrise Energy Metals for the Syerston scandium project in New South Wales, Australia — set to become the world's first primary scandium mine, with initial capacity of 60 tonnes per year of scandium oxide starting in H1 2028; and a $150 million conditional loan to Niron Magnetics, a magnet developer. The Export-Import Bank will lend $58 million to Westwater Resources, Global Advanced Metals, and 5E Advanced Materials.

Scandium is used in aerospace, defence, and automotive alloys. Nearly all current supply comes from China, Russia, and Ukraine. The US has not mined scandium since 1969. Under the Pentagon financing, the Department of War would receive a right of first offer on the Australian mine's output. The project already has a five-year supply deal with Lockheed Martin for up to 15 tonnes annually.

Trump declared the US would become 'the minerals superpower of the world.' The roundtable also featured deep-sea mining firm American Ocean Minerals, which presented Trump with a gold replica of a Pacific seabed nodule. Trump has previously signaled he may bypass the International Seabed Authority to issue international seabed mining licenses.
sections.whyItMatters: The $3 billion package is the largest single US government push on critical minerals and is directly tied to the Iran war's depletion of precision-guided munitions, which require rare earths, scandium, and other controlled materials. The Pentagon's right of first offer on Australian scandium output formalises a supply chain that bypasses China, Russia, and Ukraine — but production won't start until 2028, leaving a near-term gap. India's inclusion of scandium and rare earths in retaliatory considerations is an emerging risk.

sections.heading: Aramco's Jazan Refinery Catches Fire; Previously Halted After Houthi Attack
sections.body:
A fire broke out early Sunday at Aramco's Jazan refinery in southwestern Saudi Arabia and was later extinguished with no injuries, according to the Saudi Energy Ministry. The cause was not disclosed. The 400,000-barrel-per-day facility had been offline since July 27 following a Houthi militant attack, according to a Reuters-consulted industry note. Aramco CEO Amin Nasser said the prior attacks did not substantially impact the company's operations or finances.

The Jazan fire coincided with continued regional drone and missile threats. Saudi Arabia intercepted drones from Iraq — blamed on Iran-backed Iraqi militias — and Houthi forces have been targeting Saudi oil infrastructure as part of the broader regional escalation around the US-Iran conflict.
sections.whyItMatters: The Jazan refinery has been offline for nearly two weeks due to a Houthi attack, and the latest fire — regardless of cause — underscores the cumulative strain on Saudi energy infrastructure from multiple fronts. While Aramco's overall output has been maintained through other facilities, each disruption tightens available spare capacity in a market where Hormuz remains effectively blocked.

sections.heading: Ukraine Strikes Ilsky and Syzran Refineries as Drone War on Russian Energy Intensifies
sections.body:
Ukraine's military struck two Russian oil refineries overnight — the Ilsky refinery in Krasnodar region (processing over 6 million tonnes annually) and the Syzran refinery (8.5 million tonnes annually). A fire at Ilsky was extinguished Saturday, with local authorities attributing it to debris from a Ukrainian drone. Five people were wounded. Ukraine's Defence Intelligence confirmed the strike on Ilsky.

Russia's Defence Ministry claimed its air defences intercepted 397 Ukrainian drones overnight across multiple regions — a figure that could not be independently verified. Russia simultaneously struck Kyiv with drones and missiles, killing four people including a child.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukraine's refinery campaign is a sustained effort to degrade Russia's domestic fuel production capacity. The Ilsky and Syzran strikes add to a growing list of Russian refineries hit in recent weeks. With Russia's seaborne exports already down significantly and domestic fuel demand rising, cumulative refinery damage creates a real constraint on Moscow's ability to sustain both military and civilian fuel supplies.

sections.heading: Europe Faces Dual Fuel Crisis: Record-Low Gas Storage and Looming Diesel Shortage
sections.body:
Europe's natural gas storage levels have fallen to a record low, with net injection at just 8.5 billion cubic metres by end of July — 21% below the same period last year and the lowest since 2020, according to Gas Infrastructure Europe data cited by Politico and Reuters. Germany, which holds over 20% of EU storage capacity, is particularly behind on replenishment. Forecasts suggest European storage will reach only 76% by November — the lowest fill level since 2011, per the Financial Times.

The gas crisis is compounded by a looming diesel squeeze. Bloomberg reports that Europe faces a diesel shortage this winter, driven by reduced Middle East supply through Hormuz, limited global refining capacity, and competition from US East Coast demand. Eugene Lindell of FGE NexantECA warned that 'extremely high fixed prices' for diesel are likely, which would increase transport costs and inflation across the EU. Kpler analyst Zamir Yusof noted that Gulf Coast refineries cannot indefinitely supply Northwestern Europe, as cargoes will be redirected to the US East Coast for winter heating demand by Q1 2027.

Europe purchased a record 9.89 million tonnes of LNG from Russia in the first half of 2026, per FT — an irony that underscores the difficulty of replacing Russian pipeline gas while also sanctioning it.
sections.whyItMatters: The dual gas and diesel crisis is Europe's most acute energy challenge since 2022. At 76% storage fill by November, Europe would have minimal buffer for a cold winter or further supply disruption. The diesel shortage is particularly dangerous because it directly affects transport, agriculture, and heating — sectors that feed into inflation faster than gas. Record Russian LNG purchases highlight the structural contradiction in Europe's sanctions policy.

sections.heading: China Sanctions Seven US Entities in Retaliatory Tech Escalation
sections.body:
China's Ministry of Commerce sanctioned seven US entities and tightened export controls on drones and related technologies on Wednesday, in response to Washington's addition of 43 Chinese companies to the Uyghur Forced Labour Prevention Act entity list and the US Federal Communications Commission's ban on imported foreign-made robotic devices and power inverters.

Beijing also launched a national security investigation into imported printing and copying office equipment with foreign-made software. China called its measures 'restrained overall' and urged the US to withdraw its actions.

Eurasia Group analyst Dominic Chiu said the moves were 'calibrated to impose costs without breaking the truce' and would not derail Xi Jinping's planned visit to Washington in September. Tsinghua University fellow Sun Chenghao said the measures would 'heat up economic, trade and tech friction' but remained targeted rather than a broad escalation. However, he warned that US restrictions on Chinese AI models or cloud chip access could trigger a reassessment of the summit.
sections.whyItMatters: While these sanctions are primarily about technology, the drone export controls are directly relevant to energy — drones are central to both the Ukraine conflict and Middle East attacks on energy infrastructure. China's calibrated response keeps the Xi-Trump September summit on track, but the cycle of escalation has a clear trajectory: US restrictions on advanced chips or AI could trigger Chinese export controls on rare earths or processing technology, which would hit the critical mineral supply chains the US is simultaneously trying to build up.

bottomLine: The day crystallised a central tension in the energy order: Iran is simultaneously negotiating Hormuz access and firing missiles at Gulf tankers, demanding maximalist concessions that the US is unlikely to grant in full. The ADNOC missile strike shows Iran can disrupt Gulf shipping even while talking about reopening it. The Senate's Graham Act opens a second front — threatening 100% tariffs on India and China over Russian oil, which could split the US-India relationship at a moment when Washington needs New Delhi's cooperation on Iran. Trump's $3 billion critical minerals push acknowledges the supply chain vulnerability exposed by the Iran war's munitions burn rate, but most production won't come online until 2028. Europe's record-low gas storage and looming diesel shortage add a ticking clock: if Hormuz doesn't reopen or a cold winter hits, the energy crisis will compound across both gas and diesel simultaneously.
